prompt.context: Your client is the CEO of the Mustard Clinic, a for-profit hospital in the United States. The hospital is known primarily for its leading care for babies and young children. Patients pay a fixed fee to access services on arrival, and all subsequent costs are borne by the Mustard Clinic. The Mustard Clinic does not deal with insurance providers — patients submit expense claims directly with their insurance provider(s). In the last few years, the hospital's profitability has fallen, and they are facing bankruptcy. Last year they lost $1.4m.
prompt.question: Why has profitability gone down and how can we turn it around?

clarifying_info.a: The Mustard Clinic wants to at least break even.

clarifying_info.q: Can the clinic change its patient mix?
clarifying_info.a: The Clinic cannot influence its patient mix in the short term.

clarifying_info.q: What services does the clinic offer?
clarifying_info.a: The Clinic offers intrapartum (childbirth), neonatal (for newborns), pediatrics (for infants and children), and a small geriatrics (for the elderly) unit.

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors contributing to the problem?
clarifying_info.a: There aren't any competitors that have contributed to the Mustard Clinic's problem.

clarifying_info.q: How does the revenue model work?
clarifying_info.a: Customers are charged a fixed fee at the time of checking in. All subsequent costs are borne by the Mustard Clinic.

exhibits.title: Key hospital unit metrics
exhibits.shows: A table listing the four hospital units (Intrapartum, Neonatal, Pediatrics, Geriatrics) with their description, annual patient volume, and average length of stay in nights.

Intrapartum.description: Care of due and in-labor mothers (during labor and childbirth)

Neonatal.description: Care of premature newborns (first 28 days of life)

Pediatrics.description: Care of infants, children, and adolescents (up to age 21)

Geriatrics.description: Care of elderly patients (aged 60 and over)

exhibits.title: Cost structure
exhibits.shows: A summary of the clinic's cost structure showing fixed costs, variable cost per patient per night, average stay, total annual patients, and capacity utilization.

data.note: Capacity = Total number of patient nights per year that the Mustard Clinic can accommodate

framework: Analyze customer segments: understand the volume and average stay per unit to identify where patient-nights are concentrated
Determine cost impact of shorter stays: calculate variable cost savings from reducing average stay duration
Determine profit impact of shorter stays: calculate how freed-up capacity translates into additional patients and net profit
Brainstorm ways to shorten patient stays: use the patient journey (Admittance → Diagnosis → Surgery → Recovery → Other) to generate ideas
Provide a recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit A, calculate the overall average patient stay duration in nights and identify which unit drives the most patient-nights.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply volume by average stay for each unit to get total patient-nights, sum them, then divide by total patients. Key insight: because the clinic charges a fixed fee, longer stays increase costs without increasing revenue, so reducing average stay is a promising lever. Geriatrics has the highest average stay (25 nights) despite low volume; Intrapartum drives the most total nights (5,000).

math.setup: Total nights = sum of (volume × average stay) across all units; Average stay = Total nights / Total patients
math.answer: Average stay = 10 nights; Intrapartum generates the most patient-nights (5,000)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit B, if the Mustard Clinic reduces the average patient stay by 2 nights (from 10 to 8), what is the variable cost saving? Does this alone solve the profitability problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate variable costs under each scenario and find the saving. The saving ($1.2m) equals exactly the current loss ($1.4m loss minus fixed costs already accounted for), but does NOT fully close the gap on its own — it reduces costs but does not add revenue. The key insight is that shorter stays also free up capacity for new patients.

math.setup: Variable cost = patients × average stay nights × $600/night; Fixed costs unchanged at $1.4m
math.answer: Saving = $1.2m. This does not fully solve the problem on its own, but shorter stays free up capacity for additional patients.

questions.prompt: Reducing average stay from 10 to 8 nights frees up capacity. If average revenue per patient is $6,000, how many additional patients can be served and what is the net profit impact?
questions.guidance: Candidate must link the freed capacity (in patient-nights) to additional patients at the new 8-night average, then compute the full P&L for 1,250 patients. The result shows the clinic returns to profitability with $100k profit. Strong candidates will quickly see that this also covers the $1.4m current loss.

math.setup: Hospital capacity = 10,000 patient-nights (fixed); freed nights = 1,000 × 2 = 2,000; additional patients = 2,000 / 8; new P&L with 1,250 total patients
math.answer: 250 additional patients can be served; profit = $100k (breakeven achieved with $100k surplus)

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways in which the Mustard Clinic could reduce the average patient stay duration from 10 to 8 nights?

categories.name: Admittance
ideas: Decrease or eliminate the Geriatrics unit (high average stay of 25 nights, not core competency)
Increase receptionist staffing to speed check-in and reduce delays at admission

categories.name: Diagnosis
ideas: Partner with other hospitals for specialist diagnosis to avoid wait times
Use tele-diagnosis technology to reduce time-to-diagnosis

categories.name: Surgery / Treatment
ideas: Invest in technology to improve surgical speed and precision
Improve doctor skill and quality through training or targeted hiring
Identify and eliminate operational delays in surgical scheduling

categories.name: Recovery
ideas: Use tele-medicine or remote monitoring to allow earlier discharge
Offer structured at-home care programs (e.g., home nurse visits) as a step-down alternative
Partner with rehabilitation or step-down facilities to free up hospital beds

categories.name: Other / Structural
ideas: End fixed-fee pricing model in favor of per-night or episode-based pricing to align incentives
Drive awareness of the cost structure to doctors so they optimize discharge timing

recommendation: The Mustard Clinic can return to profitability by reducing average patient stay from 10 to 8 nights
This frees up capacity for 250 additional patients and generates $100k in net profit
A concrete first step is to close or scale down the Geriatrics unit (25-night average stay, not core competency), which alone would significantly reduce the blended average stay
risks: Reducing average stay duration could worsen patient outcomes and damage the clinic's reputation for leading care
Eliminating Geriatrics may remove a complementary service that attracts or retains other patient segments
Revenue assumptions ($6,000/patient fee) may not hold if patient mix or payer behavior changes
recommendation.risks_note: Reducing average patient stay might affect revenues if patient care worsens or if Geriatrics is a complementary service.
next_steps: Commission a feasibility study into tactical ways to reduce average stay without compromising patient care
Pilot tele-medicine and at-home care discharge pathways in one unit before rolling out broadly
Review Geriatrics unit economics in detail to assess closure viability
